# Get the population data you need

`tarr.pop` helps you retrieve population counts for selected places,
years, and demographic groups. You can return those counts as a data
frame or tibble for analysis, reporting, or plotting. This guide follows
one example: obtaining population estimates for Dallas, Tarrant, and
Travis counties for the latest five available years.

The usual workflow is to open a population cube, inspect its labels,
select the population you need, and convert the result to a table. If
you want totals rather than separate demographic groups, you sum those
groups before conversion. You do not need to understand the underlying
R classes to follow these steps.

A population cube is an array with named dimensions. A cell might contain
the number of female residents of Tarrant County aged 65 in 2022 in a
particular race/ethnicity category. The dimension labels identify which
population each count describes. The package keeps that structure and
its metadata together while you select and summarize data.

# Find and open a cube

## What you need before starting

You need the installed `tarr.pop` package and access to its population
cube files. The large HDF5 cube files live in a configured folder,
separately from the installed R package. Installing the package does not
by itself supply every cube listed below or download it from its source.
Obtain the prepared cube folder from your project or data administrator.
If you need to build cubes from source data, see the
[cube creation guide](population_cube_creation_version_2.qmd).

Load the packages used in this guide:

```{r libraries}
#| message: false
library(tarr.pop)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
```

For a first setup, point the package to the root of your prepared cube
folder, which contains the `base/` and `derived/` directories. Replace
this example path with your own. This command saves your choice for
future R sessions; it does not populate an empty folder with cube files.

```{r configure_cubes}
#| eval: false
set_cube_path("/path/to/Population/Cubes", create = FALSE)
```

Once configured, check the active folder:

```{r active_folder}
cube_path()
```

## Choose a population series

The packaged `population` lookup list provides convenient series names
organized by source. It is a guide to known series, not an inventory of
files present on your computer.

```{r series_names}
str(population)
```

Choose a source and series whose geography, time coverage, and demographic
categories fit your question. This example uses Texas Demographic Center
county estimates. TDC combines race and Hispanic ethnicity into one
`race.eth` dimension; some Census cubes instead provide separate `race`
and `ethnicity` dimensions. Do not assume every cube has the same axes.

```{r open_tdc_estimates}
pop <- open_poparray(population$texas.demographic.center$estimates)
pop
```

The lookup above resolves to `"tdc_estimates_county"`, so you can also use
`open_poparray("tdc_estimates_county")`. Opening the cube reads its metadata
and creates a disk-backed view; it does not load all population values
into memory. The printed summary describes its dimensions and source.

If opening fails, check the configured folder, the availability of the
requested cube, and its registration. After adding prepared cube files
to `base/`, `rebuild_poparray_registry()` refreshes the series registry.
It does not download missing data.

## Inspect coverage and labels

Start with the source notes and available coordinates. These operations
inspect metadata without extracting population values.

```{r inspect_cube}
source_meta(pop)
names(dimnames(pop))
dim(pop)

tail(times(pop))
head(areas(pop))
head(ages(pop))
sexes(pop)
dim_labels(pop, "race.eth")
```

`times()` and `areas()` follow the cube's time and area roles. `ages()`
and `sexes()` find dimensions by their semantic meaning. Use
`dim_labels()` when you want the labels of a specific named dimension,
including a combined classification such as `race.eth`.

For the TDC cube, the dimensions are `year`, `area.name`, `sex`,
`age.char`, and `race.eth`. The latest five years means the latest five
labels in this cube, not necessarily the latest five calendar years.
Check the source notes and labels rather than assuming coverage.

# Select your population

Suppose we want Dallas, Tarrant, and Travis counties for the latest five
available years. Select places and years first:

```{r select_counties_and_years}
target_counties <- c("Dallas", "Tarrant", "Travis")
recent_years <- tail(times(pop), 5)

pop_small <- pop |>
  dplyr::filter(
    area.name %in% target_counties,
    year %in% recent_years
  )

pop_small
```

Here, `filter()` selects labels along cube dimensions. It keeps all
combinations of the selected coordinates; it is not yet filtering rows
of a table. For another question, you could also select particular sex,
age, or race/ethnicity labels. Each filtering expression should refer
to one dimension.

Filtering is lazy: it creates a smaller view without extracting the
population values. Compare the number of cells before and after selection:

```{r selection_sizes}
c(original_cells = length(pop), selected_cells = length(pop_small))
```

You now have two choices. Keep the demographic detail if you need one
row for each group, or collapse those dimensions if you need county totals.

# Choose detail or totals, then return a table

## Keep demographic detail

When you want separate demographic groups, convert the filtered cube
directly. For example, this produces a tibble for female residents in
one selected county and year, retaining age and race/ethnicity categories:

```{r detailed_table}
selected_groups <- pop_small |>
  dplyr::filter(
    area.name == "Tarrant",
    year == recent_years[length(recent_years)],
    sex == "female"
  )

# EAGER: read this selected result into memory.
detail_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(selected_groups)
head(detail_tbl)
```

There is one row per selected cube cell, with one column for each dimension
and a value column named `population` in this series. Dimension labels may
be factors, including ordered factors for age and time. Missing counts
remain missing; an `NA` does not mean zero. Conversion preserves the cube's
categories, so an overlapping category may still appear in this detailed
table. Do not sum its rows indiscriminately.

## Calculate county totals safely

For county totals, sum over age, sex, and the combined race/ethnicity
classification. First check whether the selected categories overlap:

```{r inspect_overlap}
overlaps(pop_small)
```

The TDC cube declares `"85 +"` as an overlap level. In the recent-year
selection used here, the age labels include individual ages above 85
and the terminal `"95 +"` group. Remove the declared `"85 +"` level before
summing; the remaining age categories cover older residents. This is not
a request to exclude everyone aged 85 and older.

```{r prepare_totals}
pop_for_totals <- pop_small |>
  drop_overlap_levels(dim = "age.char")

tail(ages(pop_for_totals))
overlaps(pop_for_totals)
```

This choice is specific to the categories and period in this example.
For other cubes or older TDC periods, inspect their age labels and source
coverage before removing a group. Removing declared overlap levels does
not guarantee that all overlap has been resolved; the reduction guards
remain active. If summing is rejected, inspect the categories rather than
bypassing the guard.

Now collapse the three demographic dimensions:

```{r county_totals}
pop_totals <- pop_for_totals |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("age.char", "race.eth", "sex"))

pop_totals
```

Collapsing reads and sums values in blocks and writes a new HDF5-backed
result. It is bounded-memory computation, rather than another queued
filter. The time and area dimensions remain, while each collapsed
dimension has one level called `"all"`.

## Choose a data frame or tibble

Both conversions below are **eager**: they read the selected result into
R memory. That is why we first selected the relevant counties and years
and, for totals, collapsed the demographic detail.

```{r convert_totals}
county_df <- as.data.frame(pop_totals)
county_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_totals)
county_tbl
```

Both tables contain the same population values. Choose a data frame for
base R tools or a tibble for a tidyverse workflow. With three counties and
five years, the total table contains 15 rows. The `sex`, `age.char`, and
`race.eth` columns contain `"all"`, recording the dimensions that were summed.

For reporting, keep just the columns you need and convert the year labels
to integers. Convert through character so factor codes are not mistaken
for years:

```{r reporting_table}
county_tbl <- county_tbl |>
  dplyr::select(year, area.name, population) |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(as.character(year)))

county_tbl
```

At this point you have an ordinary in-memory table. You can join it to
other analysis data, write it to a file, or plot it using your usual R tools.

# Plot the result

```{r plot_totals}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 4.8
ggplot(county_tbl, aes(x = year, y = population, color = area.name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Population estimates for three Texas counties",
    subtitle = paste("Texas Demographic Center;", paste(range(county_tbl$year), collapse = "–")),
    x = "Year",
    y = "Population",
    color = "County"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

# How the package protects your results

The object opened above is a `poparray`. It combines an array of population
values with dimension labels, source notes, time and area roles, and
semantic metadata. DelayedArray supports deferred operations, while
HDF5Array provides disk-backed storage. Keeping the large source cube on
disk and extracting only your analysis slice avoids unnecessary memory use.

A dimension's `DimSemantics` metadata describes two separate properties.
Its partition type says whether categories are mutually exclusive or may
overlap. Its scale type says how labels should be interpreted: for example,
age groups have interval meaning rather than being arbitrary strings.
Those properties help the package reject unsafe aggregation.

```{r inspect_semantics}
time_role(pop)
area_role(pop)
dim_semantics(pop)$age.char
```

These checks cannot replace understanding the source. A metadata definition
marked as validated does not certify every count or make every sum safe.
TDC's combined race/ethnicity classification is different from separate
race and ethnicity dimensions. Likewise, Census counts, annual estimates,
and projections answer different questions. For decennial data, years such
as 2000, 2010, and 2020 are observation years, not annual coverage.

# Where to go next

Use this workflow for your next question: choose the source, inspect its
coverage, select your places and groups, decide whether to retain detail
or calculate totals, then extract a table. Keep population values on disk
until you need them, and review overlap warnings before summing.

For more detail, see the [API reference](api_reference.qmd), the
[`poparray` class guide](poparray_class.Rmd), or the
[projection introduction](poparray_projection_intro.Rmd). Function help
such as `?dim_labels`, `?filter.poparray`, and `?collapse_all` provides
argument details and examples.
